summary: On the day the Passover lambs are killed, Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the meal in a large upper room, then sits down with the Twelve.
key_insight: Jesus did not merely endure this meal on His way to the cross. He told the Twelve, “With fervent desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” He had longed for this night with them.
story: On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lambs were killed, {Mk} the disciples asked Jesus, “Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?” {Mt} He sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat.” {Lk}

He told them, “Behold, when you have entered the city, a man will meet you carrying a pitcher of water; follow him into the house which he enters.” They were to say to the master of the house, “The Teacher says to you, ‘Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?’” {Lk} Matthew gives the message this way: “My time is at hand; I will keep the Passover at your house with My disciples.” {Mt}
The man would show them a large upper room, furnished and prepared. {Mk} They went and found it just as He had said, and they prepared the Passover.

When evening came and the hour had come, Jesus sat down, and the twelve apostles with Him. {Lk} He said to them, “With fervent desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer; for I say to you, I will no longer eat of it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” {Lk}
Then He took a cup, gave thanks, and said, “Take this and divide it among yourselves; for I say to you, I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” {Lk}
differences: Luke alone names Peter and John as the two disciples sent.
Mark and Luke describe the man carrying a pitcher of water and the large upper room; Matthew says only “a certain man” and gives Jesus’ message, “My time is at hand.”
In Matthew and Mark the disciples first ask where to prepare; in Luke, Jesus sends Peter and John, and they ask Him where.
Luke alone records Jesus’ words about His fervent desire to eat this Passover and the cup shared before the bread.

fit.question: Matthew, Mark and Luke call this meal the Passover, eaten on the day the lambs were killed. But John says that on Friday morning the priests would not enter Pilate’s headquarters, “that they might eat the Passover” (John 18:28), and calls Friday “the Preparation Day of the Passover” (John 19:14). Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?

points.label: A Passover on Thursday night
points.text: Many hold that all four Gospels agree on a Thursday night Passover. In John, “the Passover” can mean the whole seven-day feast and its sacrificial meals, so the priests in 18:28 were guarding their purity for the festival meals still ahead. “Preparation Day” was the usual name for Friday, the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42; John 19:31), so 19:14 means the Friday of Passover week. McGarvey takes this view.

points.label: Two ways of reckoning
points.text: Others suggest that different groups in Jesus’ day reckoned the festival calendar differently, so that Jesus and His disciples kept Passover a day before the temple leaders did. This would let both timings stand, but clear evidence of two Passover days at the temple is lacking.

points.label: A Passover meal ahead of time
points.text: Others think Jesus, knowing He would die as the lambs were slain, held His Passover meal a day early. But Mark and Luke tie the preparations to the day “when they killed the Passover lamb,” which this view must explain.

fit.note: Faithful scholars weigh these options differently, but all agree on what matters most: Jesus shared a Passover meal with His disciples and died as “Christ, our Passover” (1 Corinthians 5:7).
fit.short: Many see a Thursday Passover, with John’s “Passover” meaning the whole feast; others propose two calendars or an early meal. Views differ.

scene.label: Passover lambs
scene.text: On the afternoon of 14 Nisan, each household’s lamb was slaughtered in the temple courts and its blood poured out at the altar by the priests. The lamb was roasted whole and eaten that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, as Exodus 12:8 commands. Peter and John had a long afternoon’s work ahead of them.

scene.label: A man with a water jar
scene.text: Drawing water was usually women’s work, so a man carrying a jar would be easy to spot in a crowded city. Jesus gave no name or street, only a sign to follow. Judas was watching for a chance to hand Jesus over away from the crowds; keeping the place unknown until evening may have kept the supper from being interrupted.

scene.label: The upper room
scene.text: A large upper room, already furnished with couches or cushions for reclining, suggests a well-to-do home. Jerusalem families opened rooms to pilgrims at Passover. Some think the house belonged to the family of John Mark, whose mother’s house later sheltered the church (Acts 12:12), but Scripture does not say.

scene.label: The first cup
scene.text: Later Jewish writings describe four cups of wine at the Passover meal, often linked to God’s four promises in Exodus 6:6–7. Luke records a cup before the bread (22:17) and another “after supper” (22:20), which fits that pattern.

witnesses.matthew: Gives the shortest account, centered on Jesus’ message to the host: “My time is at hand.” In Matthew, Jesus is the Teacher who sets the time and place, and the disciples simply do as He directed.
witnesses.mark: Gives the vivid directions: the man with the water jar and the large upper room, furnished and prepared. Mark notes that it was the day “when they killed the Passover lamb,” setting the supper beside the sacrifice.
witnesses.luke: Names Peter and John and alone records Jesus’ longing to eat this Passover “before I suffer,” with a first cup shared before the bread. Luke shows the old feast pointing forward: Jesus will not eat it again “until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.”
witnesses.john: Does not record the preparations. John tells of the evening itself, beginning with Jesus washing the disciples’ feet (13:1–20).

seeing.reveals: Jesus walks toward His suffering in full command and with deep desire. He arranges the room, directs the disciples, and longs to share the feast of the lamb with them on the eve of His own sacrifice.
seeing.living: Jesus wanted to eat with these men, knowing they would fail Him within hours. Do not keep your distance from Him because you know your weakness; He desires your company. And when His instructions seem small, like following a man with a water jar, do them, and you will find things “just as He had said.”
seeing.ponder: Do you believe that Jesus truly desires to be with you, and how would that change the way you come to Him?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus prepares the table, keeps His appointment, and longs to share it with His own.
outline: The day the lambs were killed (7–8)
A desire fulfilled at the table (14–16)
A cup pointing to the kingdom (17–18)
preaching.watch_for: Twice in three verses Jesus speaks of “the kingdom of God” (vv. 16, 18). The Passover looked back to Egypt, but Jesus turns it toward the future: this meal points to what He is about to do and to the feast still to come.
